analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayer-insured banks trade certain risky swaps again by weakening a Dodd-Frank rule that pushed them out.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 292-122 on October 30, 2013, but the Senate never voted, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 crisis, Dodd-Frank section 716 told banks: if you want FDIC insurance and Federal Reserve loans, keep risky swaps dealing in a separate affiliate that doesn't get federal backstops. This bill would undo much of that, allowing insured banks to keep certain swaps — including swaps tied to asset-backed securities, the kind that blew up in the crisis — inside the federally insured bank. The House passed it 292-122, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and foreign banks' US branches that deal swaps. The bill would let them move structured-finance and asset-backed swap dealing back inside FDIC-insured institutions and extend the federal-assistance exemption to uninsured US branches of foreign banks, sparing them the cost of housing swaps in a separately capitalized affiliate. Supporters also argued it fixes mismatches that pushed some customer hedging to less-regulated entities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big banks and foreign bank US branches

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let banks and foreign-bank US branches keep swap dealing in FDIC-insured institutions when it involves hedging, non-structured swaps, or approved structured finance swaps, instead of pushing those trades into a separate affiliate.
It would let insured banks use federal backstops while trading swaps based on asset-backed securities, either for hedging or for categories the prudential regulators jointly approve.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and bank customers generally, in the form of a restored implicit subsidy: if federally backstopped banks bet on asset-backed derivatives and lose, the FDIC and Federal Reserve stand behind them. Critics of the original pushout rule said it cost nothing, but the risk, if realized, would land on the public safety net.

drawbacks.text: By extending the federal-assistance exemption to insured banks and foreign-bank US branches doing structured finance swaps, the bill would again allow institutions backstopped by the FDIC and the Federal Reserve to trade asset-backed derivatives — the kind of activity critics said put taxpayers behind speculative trades and helped cause the 2008 crisis.

The exemption for structured finance swaps depends partly on regulators jointly writing rules approving them, but the bill writes the basic permission into statute, so regulators would have to act to hold the line rather than to expand it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated case was that the swaps pushout rule created mismatches — forcing some derivatives out of regulated banks and into less-regulated shadow markets — and that allowing banks to make markets in asset-backed securities helps borrowers. But the core effect was to let taxpayer-insured banks resume potentially risky derivatives trading that the post-crisis law had deliberately pushed out, restoring an implicit public subsidy to a profitable Wall Street activity. The Senate never weighed the trade-off, so the bill died without that debate ever being resolved.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it with a big bipartisan vote, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it, so it expired without a vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 292-122 on October 30, 2013, with 222 of 230 Republicans and 70 of 200 Democrats in favor.
An amendment offered from the floor that would have preserved regulators' ability to police manipulation of commodity markets, including oil and biofuel speculation, failed 190-223.
The Senate referred the bill to its Banking Committee on October 31, 2013, and it never received a vote or a floor action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks gained nothing in law but kept the Dodd-Frank status quo; the House-passed loosening went nowhere, so no special interest actually prevailed either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Neither side; the Dodd-Frank restriction stayed in place

for.name: Randy Hultgren
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Financial Services and Agriculture Committees.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee (53-6) and House Agriculture Committee (31-14)
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and markups and reported the bill to the House floor.

for.name: 70 of 200 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage, providing the margin that made it bipartisan on the floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 31, 2013 and took no action; it never got a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: 190 House members (mostly Democrats)
against.what_they_did: Voted 190-223 (nearly all Democrats) for a motion to send the bill back with instructions to preserve regulators' power to police commodity market manipulation, including oil and biofuel speculation; it failed.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was mostly party-line — 222 of 230 Republicans voted yes while 119 of 200 Democrats voted no — though 70 Democrats crossed over to support it, and the motion to recommit split almost purely by party (189 Democrats for, 223 Republicans against).

industries.industry: Large banks and their swap-dealing arms
industries.note: The bill would let FDIC-insured banks keep profitable structured-finance and asset-backed swap dealing inside the insured institution, with access to Federal Reserve credit and FDIC insurance restored. It reopens a Dodd-Frank restriction written after the 2008 crisis.

industries.industry: Foreign bank US branches and agencies
industries.note: Uninsured US branches of foreign banks would get the same federal-assistance exemption as insured banks, expanding who can swap inside a backstopped entity.

Supporters argued keeping swap dealing in insured banks gives customers a safer, more liquid market; the cost is that the safety comes from an implicit taxpayer guarantee rather than from the banks' own capital.
